text.p: Australian business investment figures Monday will be critical both for the outlook for the economy and monetary policy in the months ahead, analysts said.

In particular, any backtracking on investment intentions would be of major concern to the government, which is looking for 14 percent growth in 1996/97, and the Reserve Bank which has highlighted investment as the "linchpin of forecast growth".
"Any substantial slowing in the momentum here would cast serious doubt on the budget estimates for investment and GDP growth," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Tony Meer.

Forecasts for private capital expenditure (CAPEX) in the September quarter centered on a fall of 3.0 percent to A$10.06 billion, but views were wildly divergent. Estimates ranged from a rise of 2.5 percent to a fall of 15 percent.
Analysts said much depended on how the 16 percent rise reported in the June quarter was perceived as the start of a sustained pick-up or a one-off burst.

"We think it was a rogue number and CAPEX will return to the small positive trend seen previously," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia. "That's why we're going for a fall of 10-15 percent on the quarter."
But of equal importance to the actual Q3 outcome would be the survey of business expectations for investment in the whole 1996/97 fiscal year.

The Bureau of Statistics takes a number of bites at this starting in January-February of the previous financial year and updating each quarter. In this case, the September quarter figures will include the fourth estimate of CAPEX for 1996/97.

Up to now the estimates have been running very strongly with the June quarter survey showing businesses expecting a rise of 12.7 percent in nominal terms, assuming expectations turn into actual investment at the average ratio of the past five years.
"If the survey shows some winding back of investment plans, this would cast further doubt over the government's investment forecast," said Ric Simes, chief economist at Rothschilds.
"And, in doing so, strengthen the case for a further cut in interest rates."
He saw reason to expect just such a winding back in investment plans, primarily due to a sharp slowing in capital goods imports seen in the quarter.
Imports of machinery, computers and the like fell 15.3 percent in the September quarter on the previous quarter leading many economists to look for a fall in equipment CAPEX.

In the last survey, business had only looked for a modest 0.8 percent rise in spending on plant and equipment in the six months to December, so it would not take much of a pullback to see intentions turn negative, they said.
But the outlook for spending on buildings and structures was much more bullish and another upgrading in expectations was likely from the 16 percent rise foreseen in the last survey.

Rothschild's Simes noted so far this year, non-residential building approvals had risen 1.6 percent in Q1, 5.6 percent in Q2 and 12.2 percent in Q3, a trend which seemed consistent with the optimism seen in the last survey.
Engineering construction, which is about half the size of non-residential investment, was also booming with work commenced rising 30 percent in 1995/96 and still on an upward trend.
That led Rothschild to think spending on buildings could top 20 percent this year, but equipment investment would be unlikely to grow by more than five percent.

In the last survey, the expectations had been for spending of A$39.34 billion in 1996/97 and, to be consistent with government forecasts, a rise of around four percent on that was needed to A$41-42 billion in Monday's release.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
